lead: The Serranos Towers and the Quart Towers are the only two gates that survive from the Christian wall that protected Valencia for four centuries.

Medieval Valencia was surrounded by an imposing Christian wall built from 1356 during the reign of Peter IV the Ceremonious. It had four main gates and numerous secondary posterns. Of that whole defensive system, only two monuments have survived to this day: the Serranos Towers to the north and the Quart Towers to the west.

Both were declared National Historic-Artistic Monuments, have served as prisons, gunpowder stores and refuges for works of art, and today are two of the city’s most recognisable emblems. Admission to both is free.

items.kicker: Plaza de los Fueros · El Carmen district
items.title: Serranos Towers
items.subtitle: The main gate of medieval Valencia
items.body: Built between 1392 and 1398 by master builder Pere Balaguer, the Serranos Towers were the main entrance to Valencia’s walled enclosure, facing the Serrans region and the road to Zaragoza. Declared a National Historic-Artistic Monument, they are one of the best examples of 14th-century military architecture in Europe.
facts: The gate handled up to 95% of the goods entering and leaving the city. On the outer façade, a small green bronze bell – installed in 1399 – warned of dangers; it fell silent in January 1812, damaged by a Napoleonic shell, and the crack in its lower part can still be seen.
Prison for nobles and refuge for the Prado

After the fire at the municipal jail in 1586, the towers became a prison for nobles and knights, a role they kept until 1888. This use as a prison saved them when the wall was demolished in 1865. During the Spanish Civil War, their sturdiness turned them into a store for works from the Prado Museum, protecting them from the bombing of Madrid with a reinforced-concrete vault and a humidity control system.
A living symbol of the city

Today the towers are one of Valencia’s most recognisable icons. Every last Sunday of February, the fallera mayor proclaims the official opening of Las Fallas from their gateway in the event known as La Cridà. From the battlemented terraces you get some of the best views of the River Turia and the historic centre.

items.kicker: C/ Quart · C/ Guillem de Castro
items.title: Quart Towers
items.subtitle: The western gate, with the scars of war
items.body: The west façade of the medieval city, facing Castile along the road that passed through Quart de Poblet. At 34 metres high – one metre taller than the Serranos Towers – they are the best-preserved Gothic defensive towers in Europe. Their outer façade still bears the marks of the cannon fire of the Napoleonic siege of 1808: 132 cannonball impacts and more than 1,000 perforations from rifle shot.
facts: Its name comes from the Latin at quartum milliarium – four Roman miles, the distance that separated it from Quart de Poblet. It was one of the four main gates of medieval Valencia, built from 1441 to replace an earlier postern considered insufficient for the traffic of people and carts from the interior of the peninsula.

On 28 June 1808, between 8,000 and 10,000 soldiers of Marshal Moncey were halted before these towers by the defence led by Marshal Saint Marcq. Valencia withstood the siege. The traces of that bombardment were deliberately preserved during the restoration as a testimony to the city’s resistance.
From gunpowder store to women’s prison

In 1562, the Generalitat stored gunpowder inside. In 1626 they were converted into a women’s prison – the Casa Galera – a use they kept until the 19th century. Like the Serranos Towers, this use as a prison saved them when the wall was demolished in 1865. Declared National Historic-Artistic Monuments in 1931, a full restoration between 1976 and 1982 recovered their original appearance.

blocks.title: Practical information for your visit
items: Both towers are free to enter all year round
General opening hours: Tuesday to Saturday 10:00–19:00 / Sundays 10:00–14:00
The Quart Towers can be reached on foot from the Serranos Towers in 10 minutes
The Napoleonic cannonball impacts at Quart can be seen on the outer façade
From the terraces of the Serranos Towers there are views of the Turia Gardens and the historic centre
Closed on Mondays at both monuments
